Brackenmoor, north meadow
A boar the size of a hay cart. Has eaten two fences and a cart. The cart was occupied.
Brackenmoor, the sunk pool
Something in the moor pool dangles a light at night. Travelers follow it. Travelers stop.
Brackenmoor, the old cairns
A cairn that got up and walked. It eats the other cairns. Bring a hammer.
The Pinch
Drowned Observatory, the causeway
A crab that holds the causeway at low tide and takes a toll in fingers.
Fort Ashwatch, the east yard
The fort's old war-hound, still on patrol. Nobody told it the war ended. Nobody can get close enough to tell it.
The Ashen Reach, the high ridge
A gull that flew through the broken sun and came out burning. It has not stopped.
The Ashen Reach, the glass hollows
A scorpion that ate a cathedral window. You can see the saints through its back.
The Ashen Reach, far shard
It lives in the old burial shard. It speaks with the voices of the people buried there.
The Hollow Bell, the inverted nave
The abbey's choir-mistress, still conducting. The choir is gone. She has not noticed.
The Garden That Remembers, the east beds
A rose-hedge in the shape of a bride. Do not let her hold your hand.

That's every bounty on the board. Nobody's cleared it since the old man died.
The old man. Harrow — he founded this Lodge. Something killed him in a hollow south of the moor. We never posted it. We never had anyone good enough.
You might be. I've marked the Hollow on your map. Don't make me take your names off the wall.
Harrow's Hollow
Something killed the Lodge's founder. The Hollow is marked on the world map.
Every bounty. In a world like this. You know what that makes you? A reason for people to keep going.
There's one more. Not on any board. Up past the wounds, where the sky is darkest, something black hangs that isn't a wound.
The old hunters called it the Black Star. I've marked the way. Be what you've been.
The Black Star
Above the seven wounds hangs a dark star. The way is marked on the world map.
The chord sours. The tones fade. Something below sighs.
The three tones become one. Far below, the great bell answers — and the way down opens.
The white flower turns toward you and, in a voice that is not a voice:
Antlers over the door. Smoke from the chimney. Somewhere inside, a woman is shouting at a ledger.
Welcome to the Hunters' Lodge. I'm Adelind; I keep the board, the books and the peace, in that order.
People post bounties for monsters that are too much for a village. You hunt them, you bring proof, you get paid. Proof is the monster not being there anymore.
Wipe your boots.
Lodge is open. Mostly. The roof's over there now.
I was Adelind's apprentice. She went down with the north wing when the sky broke. Kept the books dry, though. She'd want me to say that.
The board still works. Monsters are worse. People need them gone more than ever.
Oh — I know your face. You hunted for her. She used to say you never wiped your boots.
Old Sill
At low tide a causeway rises out of the bay, and at its end a dome — half-sunk, green with weed, older than any Lantern.
That's not on any map I've read.
Then we're about to read a new one.
The great lens throws a bar of light up the stair. The way is open.
A great lens on a brass arm, crusted with salt. Beyond the gallery, the stairway is sealed by a curtain of pale crystal.
Turn the lens toward the stair?
Turn it
Sunlight bends through the glass and strikes the crystal. It sings — one clear note — and shatters.
That note. It is the one the Lanterns sing. But backwards.
The orrery is still now. Seven brass suns, and one empty socket in the middle.
A vast brass orrery fills the dome: seven small suns on seven arms, circling an empty socket.
Carved around the rim: _WHAT IS SUNG FORWARD CAN BE SUNG BACK. WE MEASURED IT. WE CHOSE NOT TO._
